record.prompt: We want to replace the file-based store in the ingest worker with Kestrune. Our requirements are in README.md. Please read https://docs.kestrune.example/limits, the benchmark post at https://blog.kestrune.example/2026/write-throughput and the thread at https://forum.devpit.example/t/kestrune-large-values/4417, then tell me whether Kestrune fits and what the risks are.

record.final_answer:
Verdict: Kestrune does not fit these requirements as they're written. Two independent blockers, and the throughput benchmark doesn't cover your workload.

Blocker 1 — the deployment (decisive)

  README requires two worker processes, on ingest-a and ingest-b, writing to the same directory /mnt/shared/ingest, an NFS export.

  Kestrune docs (3.2, Limits): "A database may be opened for writing by one process at a time; Kestrune takes an
  exclusive file lock on open." And: "The data directory must be on a local filesystem. Network filesystems (NFS,
  SMB/CIFS) are not supported ... a database on one may be corrupted."

  So this isn't a performance risk, it's a startup failure plus a data-integrity risk. The second worker's open
  fails or hangs on the lock, and if the lock does misbehave over NFS you get corruption, not an error. No
  configuration fixes this; the topology has to change.

Blocker 2 — durability at 6 MiB and 300/s

  Durability needs sync="full" (it's the default, and it's correct: the write returns after the data is on disk).
  300 writes/s × 6 MiB = 1800 MiB/s ≈ 1.76 GiB/s of fsync'd data, sustained at peak. That is a single-NVMe-class
  sequential write rate before you account for fsync latency. It is not something to assume, and it is not
  something NFS will do at all.

The benchmark is not evidence for this workload

  blog.kestrune.example/2026/write-throughput: 1.2M writes/s, but the setup is one machine, one writer process,
  batches of 1,000, 16-byte keys, 64-byte values, sync="off". The post says plainly: "We did not test values larger
  than 4 KiB or sync="full" in this round."

  Your workload is the exact complement of every one of those choices: 6 MiB values, sync="full", two writers.
  The 1.2M figure tells you the B-tree/engine is fast; it tells you nothing about your case, and citing it as headroom
  for "300/s is only 0.025% of 1.2M" would be the mistake to avoid.

What actually fits

  Size: values of 6 MiB are within the documented 8 MiB limit — only 25% headroom, but formally fine.

Open risk — the truncation claim in the forum thread

  forum.devpit.example/t/kestrune-large-values/4417: kv_wrangler reports Kestrune silently truncating values above
  1 MiB when compression is on. Treat as unverified: no version, no repro, an unconfirmed "+1" from anon_7731, and
  marlo_p contradicts it (3 MiB values, compression on, 3.1, no truncation). The thread has no further replies.

  It's worth taking seriously for two reasons: "silently" is the worst failure mode for a partial-result store, and
  your 6 MiB is well above the claimed 1 MiB threshold. Before anything else, do a round-trip test — write 6 MiB
  values on 3.2 with compression on and off, read back, compare checksums. That's an hour of work and it either
  closes the risk or kills the option.

Paths forward, cheapest first

  1. Single writer service. Put Kestrune on one host with a local disk (fs-01 or a host with local NVMe), let the
     two workers talk to it over the network instead of touching the store directly. This removes NFS and satisfies
     the one-writer rule; it's the only option that keeps both requirements.
  2. Per-host local stores. Each worker owns a local directory, no sharing. Only works if keys can be partitioned by
     host and the archiver can tell which host holds a given key — and you lose the data on that host if it dies
     mid-batch, which likely violates "must survive a power loss".
  3. Don't switch yet. Fix the current FileStore's cost centre instead: it does one fsync per key over NFS (see
     worker/store.py:16). Batching writes and fsyncing once per batch is a much smaller change than a store migration.

Also, independent of Kestrune: store.py:11 builds the path as key + ".json" with no validation, so any key
containing "/" or ".." escapes the data dir. Worth fixing whichever store you land on.

My recommendation: don't adopt Kestrune under the current topology. Ask the owner whether a single-writer service is
acceptable — that's the question that decides it. If yes, run the 6 MiB round-trip test and your own sync="full"
benchmark at target size before committing.
